text: The PlayStation 5 (PS5) is a home video game console developed by Sony Interactive Entertainment as the fifth iteration of the PlayStation brand. It was announced as the successor to the PlayStation 4 in April 2019 and launched on November 12, 2020, in Australia, Japan, New Zealand, North America, and South Korea, with a worldwide release one week later. The PS5 is part of the ninth generation of video game consoles, alongside Microsoft's Xbox Series X/S, which were released in the same month. The base model includes an optical disc drive compatible with Ultra HD Blu-ray discs, while the Digital Edition lacks this drive and is a lower-cost model for purchasing games exclusively through download. Both variants were launched simultaneously. Slimmer hardware revisions of both models replaced the original versions on sale in November 2023, colloquially referred to as the "PlayStation 5 Slim." A PlayStation 5 Pro model was released on November 7, 2024, featuring a GPU approximately 45% faster than the original PS5, twice as fast ray tracing performance, and an AI-driven upscaling technology called PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), enabling 4K at 60 frames per second for optimized games. The Pro model ships with 2 TB of internal SSD storage, does not include an optical disc drive or vertical stand (which can be purchased separately), and supports Wi-Fi 7 and 8K resolution output. It was priced at US$699 / £699 / €799 and launched globally on that date. The PS5's main hardware includes a custom system-on-a-chip (SoC) developed by AMD in collaboration with Sony, integrating a CPU and GPU. The eight-core CPU is based on AMD's Zen 2 architecture, built on a 7 nm process, operating up to 3.5 GHz, and the GPU is based on AMD's RDNA 2 architecture with 36 compute units running at up to 2.23 GHz, delivering a theoretical peak performance of 10.28 teraFLOPS. It supports hardware-accelerated real-time ray tracing and uses Sony's AGC graphics API. The console features a custom "boost" system based on AMD's SmartShift technology that dynamically adjusts CPU and GPU speeds. It includes 16 GB of GDDR6 SDRAM via a 256-bit interface, capable of 448 GB/s peak bandwidth, shared between CPU and GPU. The console has 825 GB of built-in solid-state storage (667 GB available to users), with a 12-channel interface providing 5.5 GB/s raw bandwidth and a dedicated decompression unit supporting zlib and Oodle Kraken formats for throughput of 8–9 GB/s, peaking at 22 GB/s. An internal M.2 SSD slot supports user-installed NVMe drives up to 8 TB, with SSD support added via a system update in September 2021. Games must be installed on the built-in SSD or an M.2 SSD, though developers may allow selective installation of features like multiplayer modes. External USB drives (up to 8 TB) are supported, but only PlayStation 4 games can be played directly from them; PlayStation 5 games must be transferred to internal or SSD storage. The standard model supports Ultra HD Blu-ray, standard Blu-ray, and DVD formats, but not CDs or 3D Blu-rays, with game discs holding up to 100 GB of data. The launch model has a two-tone design with a black central unit flanked by white side panels, blue LED accents, and can be oriented vertically or horizontally. Long air intake vents run along the front, and heat is exhausted through rear vents. The side panels are removable, allowing access to the SSD expansion slot, optional Ultra HD Blu-ray drive, and dust collection channels. Front ports include one USB-C (USB 3.1 Gen 2) and one USB-A (USB 2.0), while the rear offers two USB-A (USB 3.1 Gen 2), an HDMI 2.1 port, Gigabit Ethernet, and power. In vertical position, the optical drive model measures 390 mm high, 260 mm deep, 104 mm wide, and weighs 4.5 kg; the digital edition is slightly slimmer at 92 mm wide and initially weighed 3.9 kg. A minor revision in August 2021 (1100 series) reduced weight and eliminated the need for a screwdriver to attach the stand. A 1200-series revision in August 2022 featured a die shrink, reducing power consumption and allowing a redesigned heatsink, resulting in a lighter model (3.9 kg for optical, 3.4 kg for digital). The 2023 Slim revisions reduced the size and included 1 TB of internal storage at launch, though the Digital Edition was later reduced to 825 GB. The Slim Digital Edition was priced higher than the original, with a $50 increase in the US, and an optional Ultra HD Blu-ray drive can be purchased separately for $80. The Slim model with an optical drive measures 358 mm high, 216 mm deep, 96 mm wide, and weighs 3.9 kg; the digital edition is 80 mm wide and weighs 2.6 kg. The DualSense controller was revealed on April 7, 2020, and includes adaptive triggers with force feedback, a new built-in microphone array, and a speaker. The controller maintains the same buttons as the DualShock 4, with the "Share" button renamed to "Create" and additional content creation features. The PS5 supports backward compatibility with the majority of PlayStation 4 and PlayStation VR games and includes the PlayStation VR2 headset. Mark Cerny, the lead architect of the PlayStation console line, implemented a two-year feedback cycle after the PlayStation 4 launch, visiting first-party developers to gather input on hardware improvements. During PS5 development, a central challenge was reducing loading times, as developers like Tim Sweeney from Epic Games identified the slow I/O speed of hard disk drives as a limiting factor in game development. The PS5's custom SSD enables high-speed data streaming, significantly improving storage performance. The console's cooling system uses a 120 mm double-sided intake fan and a large heat sink with a heat pipe design, including a layer of liquid metal for improved heat transfer. It uses a 350-watt internal power supply and consumes less energy in rest mode than the PlayStation 4. Jim Ryan, then CEO of Sony Interactive Entertainment, concluded that a low-priced, reduced-spec version of the PS5, similar to Microsoft's Xbox Series S, would not succeed due to rapid obsolescence. Cerny first publicly described the console in a Wired interview in April 2019, and Sony's financial report for the quarter ending March 31, 2019, confirmed next-generation hardware was in development but would not ship before April 2020. A second Wired interview in October 2019 stated the console would ship worldwide by the end of 2020. Full specifications were revealed in an online presentation by Cerny on March 18, 2020, and a detailed "deep dive" was published by Digital Foundry on April 2. A major game library showcase planned for June 4, 2020, was postponed to June 11 due to the George Floyd protests and also premiered the PS5's external design. Sony planned a launch during the 2020 end-of-year holiday period. The release date and pricing were confirmed on September 16, 2020, with the console launching in Australia, Japan, New Zealand, North America, and South Korea on November 12, 2020, and worldwide on November 19, 2020. The console launched in the Philippines on December 11, 2020. Its release in India was delayed, with speculation over a trademark dispute involving the name "PS5," which was eventually resolved, leading to a release on February 2, 2021. It launched in Indonesia on January 22, 2021, and in China on May 15, 2021. Pre-orders opened on September 17, 2020, but caused a rush and scalping, prompting Sony to apologize on September 19, 2020 and commit to increased deliveries. Worldwide supply remained low from 2020 to 2023 due to a global chip shortage, with Sony expecting short retail stock until 2023. In August 2022, Sony announced a price increase of up to 20% in most markets except the US, citing economic, inflationary, and supply chain pressures; a US price increase took effect in August 2025. Accessories were not affected. Starting in September 2025, the Digital Edition of the PS5 Slim was downgraded from 1 TB to 825 GB of internal storage without announcement in Europe (September 13, 2025) and the US (October 3, 2025), with an announcement in Japan (November 11, 2025). Limited quantities of the PS5 Digital Edition and PS5 Pro with gray cases and special branding were released on November 21, 2024, to celebrate the brand's 30th anniversary, along with branded DualSense, DualSense Edge, and PlayStation Portal devices.

Limited quantities of the PS5 Digital Edition and PS5 Pro, featuring gray cases and special branding, were released on November 21, 2024, to celebrate the brand's 30th anniversary. Similar branded versions of the PlayStation DualSense, DualSense Edge, and PlayStation Portal were also made available. The DualSense wireless controller for the PlayStation 5 was revealed on April 7, 2020, and is based on the DualShock controller with modifications informed by discussions with game designers and players. It includes adaptive triggers with force feedback via voice coil actuators that adjust resistance for experiences like drawing an arrow from a bow. The controller retains the same buttons as the DualShock 4, with the "Share" button renamed to "Create" and additional tools for creating and sharing content. A new built-in microphone array allows players to communicate using only the controller, and the included speaker has been improved. The controller features two-tone coloring, primarily white with a detachable black piece, and its light bar is positioned on the sides of the touchpad. It supports USB-C connectivity, has a higher-rated battery, and includes an audio jack. An Easter egg features miniature versions of the four PlayStation button symbols (cross, circle, square, and triangle) on the controller's texture. The DualSense Edge (CFI-ZCP1), a more modular controller with replaceable stick modules, multiple control profiles, and the ability to relocate map inputs, was revealed by Sony in August 2022 and initially released on January 26, 2023, via PlayStation Direct, becoming available through other retailers on February 23, 2023. Accessories include a DualSense charging station, a new HD camera, a media remote control, and the Pulse 3D wireless headset, which integrates with the PS5's Tempest Engine 3D audio technology. The PS5 is backward compatible with most existing PS4 controllers and accessories for PS4 games, though some have limited functionality; Rock Band peripherals are supported since Rock Band 2, and PS5 games can use existing PlayStation Move, PlayStation Camera, PlayStation VR Aim Controller, officially licensed headsets, and specialty controllers like flight sticks and racing wheels. The PlayStation Portal, developed by Sony Interactive Entertainment and first released on November 15, 2023, is a handheld accessory for the PS5 that streams video games and media via Remote Play using Wi-Fi. It uses its built-in screen and a DualSense-like controller to control the console but does not run games or media natively. Sony announced the PlayStation VR2 for the PS5 in January 2022; it features a headset with dual OLED panels supporting 4K resolution, HDR, and 90/120 Hz refresh rates, along with two Sense controllers that include 14 embedded IR LEDs for tracking, haptic feedback, and adaptive triggers similar to the DualSense. The headset includes eye-tracking for foveated rendering and in-game features in select titles and supports finger touch detection to show thumb, index, and middle finger positions. Unlike the previous PS VR, it does not require external cameras and uses four internal cameras to track position via its USB-C cable. The PS VR2 launched on February 22, 2023, priced at $549.99 in the U.S., €599.99 in the EU, and £529.99 in the U.K., with launch games including Horizon Call of the Mountain, Gran Turismo 7, and Resident Evil Village. It is not compatible with PS VR games by default, requiring developer updates. The headset received positive reviews but later faced criticism for lack of continued support. The PS5's user interface is described as "accessible and informative," providing updates on friends' activities, multiplayer options, and single-player missions and rewards. Cerny stated that players should not have to repeatedly boot games to check updates, so these features are visible in the UI. Matt MacLaurin, vice president of UX design at PlayStation, described the redesigned interface as a "very interesting evolution of the OS" and a "100 percent overhaul of the PS4 UI," noting its speed and robust visual language. Eurogamer praised the interface for responsiveness, accessibility, clarity, and simplicity, rendered in 4K with high dynamic range. Users are greeted with a stylistic boot-up animation and new login screen, and the central design concepts from the PS4 were redesigned into a new home screen. The top of the screen features a row of applications and two upper tabs to switch between games and media. Selecting a game reveals specific activities like levels or multiplayer modes. The PlayStation Store is no longer a standalone app and is fully integrated into the home screen. The most significant change is the Control Center, accessed by pressing the PS button at the bottom of the screen. The upper section includes cards suggesting actions based on current or recent game activities, such as progress reports or challenges, with PlayStation Plus subscribers receiving hints, tips, screenshots, or videos. System-level cards offer options like store sales or user screenshots. The lower section contains a customizable row of icons including notifications, status updates, friends list, and system settings. According to internal materials reviewed by Vice, the "activities"-focused UI was designed to help players commit time to games, especially single-player titles, recognizing that many players have limited time and that activity cards help them plan gameplay. The PS5 supports multiple streaming services such as Netflix and YouTube, with support for others expected in the future. Sony Pictures Core was released in 2023, and the system includes support for PlayStation Now, Sony's cloud gaming service, while available. Sony's Remote Play application, available on PlayStation 4, Windows, iOS, and Android, was updated before the PS5 launch to allow remote play of PS5 games over a local network. In April 2021, Sony released a software update enabling users to transfer downloaded PS5 games to an external USB hard drive. A PlayStation 5 system software beta program was announced in June 2021, similar to the Xbox Insider program, allowing signed-up users to test early software updates. One of the first major features in the beta was internal SSD expansion via the M.2 port, added in July 2021. In September 2021, a software update introduced a new trophy tracker, Control Center customization, 3D audio support for built-in TV speakers, internal SSD expansion, and various UX enhancements. Game Trials were introduced in October 2021, initially available in the UK for Death Stranding: Director's Cut and Sackboy: A Big Adventure, allowing users to play full versions for a fixed time before needing to purchase the game. In March 2022, software update 5.00 added accessibility improvements such as an improved screen reader with support for mono audio, reading notifications aloud, additional language support, and a check mark for enabled settings. Voice command support was introduced for users in the U.S. and U.K., allowing control via "Hey, PlayStation," and Ukrainian language support was added. Game Base was enhanced with a new "Friends" tab, easier friend request declines, and other updates. Various improvements were made to trophies, child accounts, the home screen, and other features. On March 8, 2023, software update 7.00 added VRR support for 1440p, data transfer between PS5 consoles, voice chat on Discord, and the ability to save gameplay clips via voice (available only in English for the U.S. and U.K. at release). On September 13, 2023, software update 8.00 added Dolby Atmos support, increased M.2 SSD capacity to 8 TB (up from 4 TB), and the ability to mute the start-up beep. On March 13, 2024, software update 9.00 allowed adjustment of the PS5 power indicator brightness, added new features in Parties and Share Screen, and improved the mic input quality of the DualSense and DualSense Edge controllers using a new AI machine-learning model. On September 12, 2024, software update 10.00 introduced the Welcome hub, Party Share, personalized 3D audio profiles, adaptive controller charging, and support for enabling remote play for individual users. On March 25, 2025, software update 11.00 added full details on activity cards, support for Unicode 16.0 emojis, parental control adjustments, system performance and stability improvements, and refinements to messages and usability on certain screens. On September 17, 2025, software update 12.00 introduced a power saver for supported PS5 games and a feature allowing wireless controllers to be paired across multiple devices simultaneously. Each PS5 console comes preinstalled with Astro's Playroom, a game designed to demonstrate the DualSense controller. Games are not region locked, so purchases in one region can be played on consoles in all regions. Sony stated its commitment to supporting the PlayStation 4 community while embracing the PS5 as a major technological advancement. In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, Ryan emphasized that next-gen consoles should include features not available on previous generations and that developers should create games that take advantage of these features. General manager Eric Lempel affirmed that Sony wants to evolve every part of the experience, noting that new hardware and devices are necessary to deliver the intended experiences. Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart was highlighted as a next-gen game not possible on older hardware. Lempel assured that interest in PS4 will not end abruptly, with more titles to come. Sony's definition of distinct console generations was interpreted as a shift toward PS5-exclusive games leveraging the console's capabilities, rather than cross-generation releases. Ryan stated there should be no disappointment as PS5 versions take advantage of advanced features and initially planned free upgrades for PS4 versions. Few major games, such as Horizon Forbidden West, are developed as concurrent releases for both PS5 and PS4, and Sony supports publishers offering enhanced PS4 versions at no additional cost. However, in May 2021, Sony announced a shift, with Gran Turismo 7 and God of War Ragnarök now available on both PS5 and PS4, a move attributed to the global semiconductor shortage affecting PS5 availability. Sony initially planned to charge PS4 users to upgrade to the PS5 version of Horizon Forbidden West upon preorder, but after negative consumer feedback—since Sony had previously stated the upgrade would be free—reversed course and made the upgrade free, though all future PS4 to PS5 upgrades from first-party games will be at cost. Eurogamer reported that Sony's certification program, as of May 2020, required PS4 games submitted after July 13, 2020, to be natively compatible with the PS5. Hideaki Nishino, Sony's senior vice president of Platform Planning and Management, stated that the PS5 is backward compatible with over 99% of PS4's 4,000+ game library, playable from launch. The console is compatible with PlayStation VR. Due to its high-speed SSD and increased processing power, many PS4 games benefit from faster loading times, improved gameplay speeds, higher or more stable frame rates, and potentially higher resolutions. Players can synchronize saved game files via cloud storage or transfer them using a USB device to avoid losing progress. Backward compatibility is enabled by hardware similarities, such as "extra logic" in the RDNA 2 GPU that ensures compatibility with PS4's GCN-based GPU. Mark Cerny explained during a March 2020 presentation and in interviews with Digital Foundry that CPU clock timing required special attention; while the Zen 2 CPU supports the PS4's Jaguar CPU instruction set, timing differences required close collaboration with AMD to match Jaguar's performance. Some PS4 games may exhibit errors when played on the PS5, and backward compatibility does not include games from previous generations. However, older PlayStation games are available through the PlayStation Plus game streaming service. The PS4's Share menu cannot be displayed, but the PS5's Create menu can be used to capture screenshots or video. All compatible downloaded PS4 games are visible in the PS5 library and available for download, can be copied via USB or Wi-Fi, and save data can be copied similarly or via cloud storage. On October 9, 2020, Sony released a list of ten PS4 games identified as incompatible with the PS5; the list has since shortened as developers released compatibility updates. As of December 16, 2021, six PS4 games remain incompatible: Afro Samurai 2: Revenge of Kuma Volume One, Hitman Go: Definitive Edition, Just Deal With It!, Robinson: The Journey, Shadwen, and We Sing. The PlayStation 4 bundled game, The Playroom, is also not supported. The PS5 was generally well received at launch, with praise for the DualSense controller's improved haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. Astro's Playroom, preinstalled on every PS5 and designed to demonstrate the controller, was praised by Laptop Mag as "deceptively cute." The exclusive launch lineup, including Spider-Man: Miles Morales and Demon's Souls, was highly praised, though some reviewers, such as TechRadar, felt there should have been more launch titles. The user interface was generally praised for being fast and easy to navigate. Many reviewers found the console's design polarizing; CNET described the black and white scheme as "clearly meant to be a sculptural conversation piece," while Tom's Guide criticized the large size as "inelegant," and others found it frustrating to integrate into a home entertainment center. However, many acknowledged the size improved cooling and reduced noise. The comparatively small 667 GB of usable SSD space was also criticized.

The PlayStation 5 was generally well received at launch, with widespread praise for its DualSense controller's improved haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. The preinstalled game Astro's Playroom, designed to showcase the controller's features, was lauded by Laptop Mag as "deceptively cute." The exclusive launch lineup, including Spider-Man: Miles Morales and Demon's Souls, was highly praised, though some reviewers, like TechRadar, noted there should have been more launch titles. The console's user interface was generally commended for being fast and easy to navigate. However, the console's design was seen as polarizing; CNET described its black and white scheme as "clearly meant to be a sculptural conversation piece," while Tom's Guide criticized the large size as "inelegant," and others found it frustrating for home entertainment integration. Despite this, many acknowledged the size helped improve cooling and reduce noise. The comparatively small 667 GB of usable SSD space was criticized. Technical reviews, such as those by Digital Foundry, noted that features like variable refresh rate and 8K video output were not available at launch, but praised the ray tracing, SSD speed, and 120 Hz output capabilities. The PS5 faced limited supply at launch and throughout 2021 due to a global semiconductor shortage and increased demand driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, with Sony expecting supply to remain limited until at least 2022. Scalpers exploited the shortage, attempting to sell consoles for thousands of dollars, prompting Sony to expand its PlayStation Direct program to sell consoles directly to consumers in Europe in November 2021 to bypass scalpers. Two weeks after launch, Sony declared the largest launch in PlayStation history, surpassing the PlayStation 4's 2.1 million units sold in its first two weeks in 2013. In Japan, during its first week of release, 103,901 standard consoles and 14,181 Digital Editions were sold, totaling 118,082 units, making it the best-selling console in the country that week; by September 2021, Sony reported over a million PS5 sales in Japan, compared to its predecessor, which did not reach a million units until a year after release. In the UK, the PS5 was the best-selling video game console in November. In Spain, it sold over 43,000 units in its first week. Sony reported 4.5 million PS5 shipments through its fiscal quarter ending December 31, 2020, similar to the PS4's launch shipments. By March 31, 2021, total shipments reached 7.8 million, surpassing the PS4's 7.6 million units in its first two quarters. As of July 18, 2021, 10 million PS5 units had been sold, marking the fastest-selling console in PlayStation history. Sony later confirmed that by June 30, 2021, it had shipped 10.1 million consoles, indicating nearly every shipped unit was sold immediately. Shipments surpassed 13.4 million by September 30, 2021. In August, Sony anticipated shipping over 22 million units by the end of its 2021 fiscal year in March 2022, but revised this to 15 million units in November. Despite the revision, sales during the 2022 fiscal year were forecast to reach 22.6 million units. Bloomberg News reported in January 2022 that Sony continued PS4 production to help alleviate the PS5 shortage during the ongoing chip shortage. By the end of September 2024, total PS5 shipments had reached 65 million units. Sony's Q2 2025 financial results stated that the PlayStation 5 had shipped 84.2 million units. Sales reached 20 million units by May 2022, 40 million by July 2023, 50 million by December 2023, and 75 million by February 2025.
